title: Deployments: blue-green, canary, feature flags, migrations, rollbacks
scopeHtml: Scope: Rolling, blue-green, canary, feature flags, expand-contract schema migrations, rollbacks, strategy choice. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Deployment goals and the risk model
notes.html:
A deployment strategy decides how new code replaces old code while users keep using the system. The goals: zero (or near-zero) downtime, small blast radius when something is wrong, and a fast way back.

Two ideas drive every strategy:

  • Deploy is not release. Putting code on servers (deploy) and turning on behaviour for users (release) can be separated with feature flags.
  • Limit blast radius. Show new code to 1% of traffic first, so a bug hurts 1% of users for 5 minutes, not 100% for an hour.

Risk grows with batch size: a deploy with 1 small change is easy to reason about and revert; a release of 200 commits is not. That is why elite teams deploy many small changes per day (DORA research: change failure rate and time to restore are lower with small frequent releases).

Worked example. At 2,000 req/s with a 1% canary, 20 req/s hit the new version. If errors are 5% on the canary, only about 1 req/s fails; the alert fires within minutes and the canary is reverted. Same bug at 100% would fail 100 req/s.

Industry examples. Amazon deploys to production every few seconds across the company (reported publicly); Netflix uses Spinnaker with automated canary analysis (Kayenta); Facebook ships the web app multiple times a day with gradual exposure and flags; Etsy popularised continuous deployment.

Everyday analogy. Replacing the engine of a moving bus: you want a plan that never leaves passengers stranded, and a way to switch back if the new engine sputters.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing a strategy without naming the rollback path.
  • Treating all changes (config, code, schema) as equally risky.
  • Skipping the metrics that decide whether to continue or abort.

notes.title: Rolling deployments
notes.html:
A rolling update replaces instances a few at a time, so old and new versions run side by side during the rollout.

Kubernetes default (strategy: RollingUpdate) with 10 replicas, maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 25%: it adds up to 3 new pods, removes up to 2 old ones, waits for readiness, and repeats.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 0   # never drop below desired capacity
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: registry/api:2.4.1
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
          periodSeconds: 5
        lifecycle:
          preStop: { exec: { command: ["sleep","10"] } }   # let LB drain
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Key requirements:

  • Readiness probes so traffic only goes to pods that are ready.
  • Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests (preStop sleep + grace period) otherwise users see 502s on every deploy.
  • Backward compatibility: old and new versions coexist, so APIs and DB schema must work with both.

Trade-offs. Cheap (no double capacity beyond surge) and the default. Slow rollback (roll forward again, same speed), and during the rollout you cannot tell cleanly which version caused a problem.

Decision gravity. Rolling is a reversible, low-effort default; the one-way part is whether your code tolerates mixed versions. If it does not, you need blue-green or a maintenance window.

Industry examples. Kubernetes Deployments, AWS ECS rolling updates, Amazon ASG instance refresh.

Everyday analogy. Replacing the carriages of a train one at a time at each station while it keeps running.

Common interview traps.

  • No readiness probe: traffic hits a pod that is still warming up.
  • Ignoring connection draining and long-lived WebSocket connections.
  • Assuming old and new never run together.

notes.title: Blue-green deployments
notes.html:
Blue-green runs two full environments: blue (current, live) and green (new). You test green, then switch all traffic from blue to green at once; rollback is switching back.

Mechanics: deploy v2 to green, run smoke tests against green with internal traffic, flip the load balancer target group / DNS / ingress selector, watch metrics, keep blue for 30 to 60 minutes (or longer) before decommissioning.

Switch options:

  • LB target group swap (AWS ALB listener rules): near instant, 0 DNS caching issue.
  • DNS weighted records: slow due to TTL and clients caching DNS (60 s TTL is often ignored by some clients).
  • Kubernetes Service selector change or Argo Rollouts blue-green.

Worked example. Service uses 20 pods (4 vCPU each). Blue-green needs 40 pods during the switch, so double the cost for that window. With cloud autoscaling the extra capacity exists for an hour, costing a small fraction of the monthly bill.

Trade-offs.

  • Pros: instant, clean rollback; test with production-like infrastructure before switching.
  • Cons: double capacity; shared resources (the database) are NOT duplicated, so schema changes must work with both versions; in-flight sessions and caches reset; all users switch at once (no gradual exposure).

Decision gravity. Good where instant rollback matters and the system is stateless. For stateful parts the database is the shared one-way door: both colours talk to the same DB, so migrations must be backward compatible (see migrations section).

Industry examples. AWS CodeDeploy blue/green, Elastic Beanstalk "swap environment URLs", Cloud Foundry, Argo Rollouts. Martin Fowler's description popularised the term.

Everyday analogy. Two identical stages in a theatre: set up the next play on the empty stage, then rotate the audience's view to it.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the shared database.
  • Saying blue-green is free; it needs double capacity.
  • DNS-based switching with long TTL leaving users on blue for minutes.

notes.title: Canary releases
notes.html:
A canary release sends a small slice of real traffic (1%, 5%, 25%, 100%) to the new version and automatically checks its health before expanding. Named after canaries in coal mines.

Gates compare canary vs baseline on: error rate, p99 latency, saturation, and business metrics (checkout conversion, crash-free sessions). Compare with a fresh baseline deployment of the old version, not the long-running fleet, to avoid cold-cache bias.

# Argo Rollouts canary with pauses and automatic analysis
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 5
      - pause: { duration: 10m }
      - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: error-rate-and-p99 }] }
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause: { duration: 15m }
      - setWeight: 100

Choosing who is in the canary: random percentage, by region (smallest region first), by internal employees first (dogfooding), or sticky by user ID (so one user sees consistent behaviour). Use sticky assignment when a user flipping between versions would confuse them or corrupt state.

Worked example. 100,000 req/s globally. 1% canary = 1,000 req/s: enough to detect a 2% error rate within about a minute (20 errors/s), while a 0.01% rate would need much more time or traffic. Choose steps and wait times by traffic volume to get statistically meaningful data.

Industry examples. Netflix automated canary analysis (Kayenta, open sourced with Google); Google and Facebook release to a small datacenter or user group first; Android app staged rollouts on Google Play (1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%) with crash-free rate watch; Istio/Envoy and AWS App Mesh do weighted routing.

Decision gravity. Canary is reversible (just set weight to 0) but needs good metrics and automation, which is the real investment. Compared to blue-green, it has the smallest blast radius but takes longer and needs mixed-version compatibility.

Everyday analogy. Restaurants testing a new dish on one table before putting it on the whole menu.

Common interview traps.

  • Canary with too little traffic to detect anything.
  • Comparing the canary to a long-warmed baseline.
  • Having no automatic abort; a human noticing at 3am is not a gate.

notes.title: Feature flags
notes.html:
A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns code paths on or off without redeploying. It separates deploy from release.

Types:

  • Release flags: hide incomplete work (trunk-based development), short lived.
  • Experiment flags: A/B tests with user bucketing.
  • Ops flags / kill switches: disable an expensive feature under load; long lived.
  • Permission flags: enable for a plan or a customer.
// Evaluate a flag with a stable user bucket and a safe default
fun isNewCheckoutOn(userId: String): Boolean {
    val rollout = flags.percent("new_checkout")          // e.g. 10
    val bucket = (murmur3(userId + ":new_checkout") and 0x7fffffff) % 100
    return bucket < rollout                              // same user -> same answer
}

Design points:

  • Stable bucketing: hash(user + flag name) so a user keeps the same experience as the percentage grows.
  • Default off and fail safe: if the flag service is down, use a cached last-known value or the safe default.
  • Local evaluation: SDKs download rules and evaluate in-process (microseconds), not a network call per check.
  • Clean up: stale flags become tech debt. Knight Capital (2012) lost about 440M USD in 45 minutes when old code behind a reused flag was activated on one un-updated server.

Mobile angle. On Android, flags fetched at app start (Firebase Remote Config, LaunchDarkly) allow turning off a broken feature in already-installed apps without waiting for a Play Store review. Keep fetch caching and defaults in the app; a server-side kill switch is a major safety net.

Decision gravity. Introducing flags is cheap and reversible; flag combinations grow (2^n states), so enforce expiry dates and owners. Build-vs-buy (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, Split) is a moderate decision; hide it behind an interface.

Industry examples. Facebook Gatekeeper, Flickr (early adopter of "flags" as continuous deployment tool), GitHub (Flipper), LaunchDarkly and Unleash.

Everyday analogy. A light switch wired in advance: the cables are installed (deployed) but the lamp stays off until you flip the switch (release).

Common interview traps.

  • Not removing old flags.
  • Per-request remote evaluation adding latency and a new failure point.
  • Random (non-sticky) assignment causing users to flip behaviour on every request.

notes.title: Database schema migrations without downtime
notes.html:
The database is shared by old and new code, so a schema change must work with BOTH versions during the rollout. Use the expand and contract (parallel change) pattern.

Steps to rename column fullname to display_name:

  1. Expand: add the new nullable column display_name. Old code ignores it.
  2. Deploy v2 that writes BOTH columns and still reads the old one (or reads new with fallback).
  3. Backfill existing rows in batches (e.g. 10,000 rows per batch with a pause) to avoid long locks and replication lag.
  4. Deploy v3 that reads only the new column.
  5. Contract: stop writing the old column, then drop it in a later release once rollback is no longer needed.
-- 1. Expand (fast, no table rewrite in modern Postgres for nullable column without default)
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;

-- 3. Backfill in small batches
UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname
WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND display_name IS NULL;

-- Build indexes without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_display_name ON users(display_name);

-- 5. Contract, much later
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN fullname;

Dangerous operations (Postgres/MySQL examples; confirm per version):

  • ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT rewrote the whole table before Postgres 11; since 11, a constant default is metadata-only.
  • CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes.
  • Adding NOT NULL or a foreign key validates the table under a strong lock; add as NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT.
  • Long ALTER waiting for a lock queues behind a long transaction and blocks all later queries: set lock_timeout (e.g. 3 s) and retry.
  • MySQL: use online DDL or tools such as gh-ost (GitHub) or pt-online-schema-change for big tables.

Worked example. Backfilling 200M rows in batches of 10,000 with a 100 ms sleep = 20,000 batches, around 33+ minutes plus query time; this avoids one 20-minute transaction that would block vacuum and spike replica lag.

Rollback. The point of expand-contract is that the code can be rolled back at any step because the old column still exists. Dropping data (contract) is the one-way door: do it only after the new version has been stable for days or weeks, with a backup.

Industry examples. GitHub gh-ost, Shopify's ghostferry and online migration practices, Stripe's four-step online migration write-up, Percona pt-osc, Django/Rails/Flyway/Liquibase tooling with "strong migrations" linters.

Decision gravity. Expand-contract costs 3 to 5 releases for one rename, a deliberate price for safety. Alternatives: maintenance window (simple, downtime), or versioned views. Destructive steps are one-way doors.

Everyday analogy. Building a new bridge beside the old one, moving traffic across, and only then demolishing the old bridge.

Common interview traps.

  • Renaming or dropping a column in the same release that stops using it.
  • CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a hot table.
  • Not setting lock_timeout, causing a lock queue outage.
  • Migrations and code deployed as one atomic step (they never are).

notes.title: Rollbacks, roll-forward and deployment safety nets
notes.html:
Rollback means going back to the previous version; roll-forward means fixing quickly with a new version. Both need to be rehearsed.

When rollback is easy: stateless code, backward compatible schema, flags to disable, artifacts for old versions retained, config versioned.

When it is NOT: after a destructive migration; after the new version wrote data in a format the old version cannot read; after external side effects (emails sent, payments charged); after a protocol upgrade (e.g. a new Kafka message schema that consumers cannot parse).

Safety nets:

  • Automated rollback on SLO burn: canary analysis aborts and reverts.
  • Kill switches via flags (fastest: seconds).
  • Immutable artifacts (container image tagged by git SHA), so rollback is kubectl rollout undo deployment/api.
  • Backward and forward compatible data formats: Protobuf/Avro schema rules (add optional fields only), tolerant readers.
  • Version skew testing in CI: run v(n) client with v(n+1) server and vice versa.
  • Deploy freezes at peak times and good deployment windows (not Friday evening).
  • Post-deploy verification: smoke tests and synthetic checks.
# Kubernetes quick rollback and history
kubectl rollout history deployment/api
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=17
kubectl rollout status deployment/api

Worked example. MTTR goal under 10 minutes: alert within 2 min (burn-rate page), human decides within 3 min, rollout undo takes 3 min for 20 pods with maxSurge 25%, verification 2 min. A flag kill switch would shave that to under 1 minute.

Real incident pattern. CrowdStrike (July 2024): a faulty content update was pushed to all endpoints at once without staged rollout; systems crashed on boot and could not self-recover. Lessons widely cited: staged rollout even for data/config updates, and make recovery possible without remote access.

Decision gravity. Make every release reversible by design; the places where you cannot (data deletion, external side effects) deserve extra review and slower rollout.

Everyday analogy. A climber's rope and anchors: you only move up once the last anchor held, so a slip never means a long fall.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming rollback is always possible.
  • Config and data changes bypassing the safe rollout process.
  • Rolling back code while the schema has already moved on.

notes.title: Choosing a strategy
notes.html:
Strategy Blast radius Rollback speed Extra capacity Needs mixed versions OK? Good for
Recreate (stop all, start new) 100%, with downtime Slow None No Dev, batch jobs, breaking changes
Rolling Grows during rollout Medium Small surge Yes Default stateless services
Blue-green 100% at switch Instant 2x Not during switch (only DB) Critical flip, simple stateless
Canary 1% then grows Fast Small Yes High traffic, risky changes
Feature flag Per user/segment Instant None Yes Decoupling release from deploy
Shadow (traffic mirroring) 0% users n/a Extra n/a Validating a rewrite with real traffic

Shadow / dark launch. Mirror a copy of production traffic to the new version and discard its responses (GitHub's Scientist library compares old and new results for refactors). Great for rewrites; beware side effects (the shadow must not send emails or charge cards).

Mobile apps. You cannot roll back installed apps. Use Play Store staged rollouts, force-update/min-version gates, flags with server kill switches, and backend backward compatibility for old app versions (often 6 to 12 months).

Industry examples. Etsy/Flickr (flags), Netflix (canary plus red/black deployments, their term for blue-green), Facebook (gradual rings), Google Play staged rollouts.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking one strategy for everything.
  • Forgetting that old mobile clients stay alive for months.
  • Shadowing traffic without disabling side effects.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Deploy is not release; use flags to decouple. Small, frequent changes reduce risk.
  • Rolling: default, needs readiness probes, graceful shutdown, mixed-version compatibility.
  • Blue-green: instant switch and rollback at 2x capacity; the shared database is the catch.
  • Canary: small traffic slice with automated metric gates; best blast-radius control.
  • Feature flags: stable bucketing, safe defaults, local evaluation, cleanup; kill switches matter for mobile.
  • Schema changes: expand, dual write, backfill in batches, switch reads, contract later; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, lock_timeout, gh-ost for big MySQL tables.
  • Plan rollback before deploying; destructive data changes and external side effects are one-way doors.
  • Combine strategies (canary then flag ramp-up) and watch SLO burn to decide to continue or abort.
